**ABSTRACT**  
Financial mismanagement remained a critical and documented challenge among Filipino households, compounded by limited access to accessible, localized, and intelligent financial tools. This study aimed to: (1) assess the financial management practices, budgeting challenges, and expense-tracking behaviors of parents aged 35–55 and young professionals aged 21–35 in San Fernando City, La Union; (2) design and develop SmartSpend, an AI-assisted mobile financial tracking and advisory application for Android; and (3) evaluate the usability of the developed system using the System Usability Scale (SUS).

The study employed a quantitative descriptive developmental research design. A validated survey questionnaire was administered to assess financial practices and technology acceptance. SmartSpend was developed using an Agile Kanban methodology, integrating a multi-provider large language model (LLM) architecture with Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite as the primary model, enabling 34 autonomous financial management actions. Usability was evaluated using the 10-item Brooke (1996) SUS instrument administered after respondents used the application for at least 10 minutes.

The needs assessment revealed that 96.7% of respondents expressed positive intent to use an AI-powered financial application, and 93.3% already used GCash, validating the target features. SmartSpend version 3.1.0 was successfully developed as an offline-first Android application with multi-modal expense input, a Financial Health Score (FHS) formally classified as a Prototype Observed Financial Health Indicator, and an eight-model cloud failover chain (Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite as primary, seven fallbacks). Usability evaluation yielded a mean SUS score of 61.83 (SD \= 17.58), corresponding to a grade of D and an adjective rating of “OK” under the Bangor et al. (2009) scale below the 68-point benchmark (Sauro & Lewis, 2016\) and the pre-established target of 80\.

The results indicated that SmartSpend showed promise as a prototype AI-assisted financial tool for the target demographic, though the below-target usability score highlighted areas for UI/UX refinement. The study contributed a locally contextualized, evaluated prototype that addressed gaps in existing Philippine personal finance applications, particularly the absence of Filipino-English LLM integration, offline-first operation, and behavioral health scoring. Nine recommendations were identified for future development, including UI/UX refinement, a backend API proxy, on-device AI, SQLite encryption, formal parsing evaluation, and a longitudinal study.

**Chapter I**

## **INTRODUCTION**

This chapter presented the background of the study, including the context and motivation for developing the SmartSpend mobile application. It also discussed the objectives of the research, scope and limitations of the system, and its intended purpose and users. In addition, this chapter outlined the conceptual framework that guided the system design, as well as the technical background of the technologies used in the development of the developed AI-powered financial assistant.

## **Project Context**

Financial mismanagement was a documented and pressing problem in the Philippines. According to the 2021 Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) Financial Inclusion Survey, only 2% of Filipino adults correctly answered all six basic financial literacy questions covering numeracy, interest rates, inflation, and risk while fewer than half reported maintaining any household or personal budget (Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, 2021). The Philippine Statistics Authority Family Income and Expenditure Survey (PSA FIES, 2021\) further revealed that a substantial proportion of Filipino households spent beyond their monthly income, with recurring expenditures on food, transportation, and utilities consistently outpacing savings. In Filipino households, parents aged 35 to 55 typically served as primary financial decision-makers, managing budgeting, bill payments, and daily expenses, yet national survey data indicated that many adults still lack formal financial accounts and did not maintain written budgets, leaving household finances managed without structured tools or guidance (Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, 2021; Philippine Statistics Authority, 2021). Despite high mobile phone penetration in the country and growing global mobile app adoption (Statista, 2024), most Filipinos did not use structured financial management tools, citing manual effort, poor local language support, and lack of meaningful feedback as primary barriers to adoption (BSP, 2021; World Bank, 2022). Secondary analyses estimated that only around one in four Filipino adults met international financial literacy benchmarks far below neighboring countries such as Malaysia and Singapore where rates exceeded 50% (Inquiro, 2024).

More recent data suggested this picture was beginning to shift, though unevenly. BSP's newer, annual Consumer Finance and Inclusion Survey (CFIS) 2025 reported that 74% of Filipinos now correctly answered basic financial literacy questions, up from 69% in 2021, alongside a reported decline in informal borrowing (Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, 2025). The same survey reported formal account ownership actually fell to 50% of adults, down from 56% in 2021 even as BSP's related Consumer Expectations Survey found household-level financial access rising to 85%, up from 74% in 2024 suggesting access was broadening at the household level while individual account ownership and structured budgeting habits remained uneven. This mixed picture, rather than a resolved problem, remained the motivation for this study.

Several studies and reports highlighted persistent challenges in personal financial management among Filipino households. National financial inclusion surveys reported that many adults had difficulty maintaining formal budgets, tracking expenses consistently, and building emergency savings, particularly in lower-income and older age groups (Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, 2021). These challenges were compounded by volatile prices, rising living costs, and the prevalence of informal credit arrangements, such as borrowing from relatives or neighborhood stores, which were often not recorded systematically in any tool or system (Philippine Statistics Authority, 2021; Flores, 2025).

A study on the financial freedom of Filipino workers further revealed pervasive literacy challenges, including reliance on traditional saving methods, high debt dependence, and a 'come-what-may' attitude toward financial planning  all of which contributed to weak financial resilience among Filipino households (Flores, 2025).

In the context of everyday life, parents and working adults frequently juggled multiple roles, including employment, caregiving, and managing household responsibilities. This left limited time and mental energy for manual expense recording or detailed financial planning. Traditional approaches, such as notebooks, spreadsheets, and simple expense trackers, relied heavily on user discipline and did not provide proactive feedback when spending patterns became risky. As a result, many users abandoned these tools after an initial trial period, leading to incomplete records and a lack of useful historical data for decision-making (Stefanov et al., 2024; Flores, 2025).

![][image1]

**Figure 1: Financial Literacy Rates by Demographic Group (BSP, 2021; Inquiro, 2024).**

Figure 1 presents the financial literacy rates across demographic groups in the Philippines, based on data from the BSP Financial Inclusion Survey (2021) and Inquiro (2024). The chart shows that only 2% of all Filipino adults correctly answered all six basic financial literacy questions, with rates varying by age group, while fewer than half of adults across most groups maintained a household budget. These figures highlight the persistent financial literacy gap that motivated the development of SmartSpend as a tool to support everyday financial management for parents and young professionals.

Globally, a variety of personal finance applications had emerged, including zero-based budgeting tools, multi-account financial dashboards, and AI-assisted expense trackers. However, many of these systems were designed for markets with widespread bank connectivity and higher levels of financial literacy, and they often depended on direct bank integration or credit card data feeds (Stefanov et al., 2024). In the Philippine context, existing applications and local solutions addressed specific aspects of financial management but still lacked integrated conversational AI, spending behavior analysis, and health scoring tailored to Filipino users who relied on mixed payment methods such as cash, e-wallets, and informal credit (Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, 2021; Stefanov et al., 2024). At the demographic level, parents and young professionals might download budgeting apps but discontinued use when the effort of manual encoding was perceived as too high and when warnings could be ignored without visible consequences for their financial standing. Table 1 presented a three-level summary of the identified gaps and SmartSpend's corresponding solutions.

**Table 1: Three-Level Gap Analysis of SmartSpend**

| Gap Level | Existing Problem | SmartSpend Solution |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| International | Manual entry dominated; AI categorization degraded for non-English transactions (Stefanov et al., 2024\) | LLM-based parsing for Filipino-English natural language input |
| National (PH) | Local apps lacked LLM chat, spending behavior analysis, and health scoring (Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, 2021; Stefanov et al., 2024\) | Conversational AI \+ Financial Health Score \+ multi-period summaries |
| Demographic | Parents abandoned apps due to manual effort; warnings were ignored without consequences (BSP, 2021\) | Automated input \+ score decay consequence system |

Several existing applications demonstrated how mobile tools could support personal financial management but also revealed gaps that SmartSpend intended to address. Tarsi – Budget Tracker, a recently introduced application available in the Philippine App Store, supported offline expense tracking, receipt image capture, and category-based summaries, which made it suitable for users who preferred manual or semi-automatic tracking (Tarsi – Budget Tracker, 2026). However, it did not provide a conversational assistant that could interpret natural language commands, nor did it compute a unified financial health score that reflected overall budgeting behavior. YNAB (You Need A Budget) implemented a zero-based envelope budgeting method that was effective for debt payoff planning, but required manual entry and a subscription cost that might have been less accessible to Filipino users (Yomio, 2026). Monarch Money offered multi-account aggregation and net worth tracking but was designed for bank-connected markets and did not support offline functionality or Filipino locale inputs. Copilot provided AI-based expense categorization but was limited to iOS and did not support Filipino-English voice or OCR input. PocketGuard simplified available spending into a single daily figure but lacked spending behavior analysis, health scoring, or multi-modal input. These comparisons demonstrated the value of existing digital financial tools but confirmed that there was still room for a localized solution that combined offline capability, multi-modal expense input, and an accessible behavioral scoring mechanism. Table 2 summarized the key feature differences.

Beyond the applications summarized in Table 2, several other Philippine-context finance apps competed in this space and were acknowledged here rather than treated as a gap SmartSpend uniquely filled. Agila: Finance Coach added a business profile (invoices, inventory, collections) on top of personal tracking, with offline-first storage and no mandatory account (Agila: Finance Coach, 2026); PISO Budget Tracker offered fully offline, ad-free, payday-cycle budgeting (PISO Budget Tracker, 2026); Lista provided salary-cycle budgeting with third-party credit-score access (Lista, 2026); Kibo auto-suggested expense categories from text, receipts, or banking alerts (Kibo, 2026); and BunnyWise targeted a broader investment dashboard (PSE and US stocks, UITFs, Pag-IBIG MP2, gold, crypto) rather than day-to-day expense tracking (BunnyWise, 2026).

GCash Pera Coach, an AI financial-literacy coach embedded in the GCash e-wallet (GCash / Mynt, 2026), was a related but distinct product: it answered financial-literacy questions on demand but did not track expenses or compute a health score. None of these offered SmartSpend's combination of Taglish conversational AI, a Financial Health Score, and multi-modal (voice, OCR, barcode, batch-screenshot) input in one offline-first app, and none were put through the same hands-on test protocol as the apps in Table 2; they were acknowledged here so that SmartSpend's contribution would be read as an evaluated integrated prototype bundle rather than a claim of being the first or only Filipino finance app.

Building on the gaps identified in the literature and the feature comparison above, SmartSpend addressed this gap by integrating a large language model (LLM) API for natural language expense parsing, a conversational AI assistant capable of executing financial actions, and a Financial Health Score (FHS) that quantified a user's financial behavior on a scale of 0 to 100\. The system operated offline using a local SQLite database with optional Firebase cloud synchronization, and supported voice, receipt OCR, barcode, and manual text AI chat, and a unified Smart Import system  including batch screenshot import that automatically detected 40+ platform types (GCash, Shopee, Steam, Lazada, GrabFood, and more) as input methods. Additionally, the application supported bulk transaction import through AI-powered text parsing, allowing users to paste transaction histories from digital wallets such as GCash and Maya, or from bank statements in various formats, for automatic parsing and categorization. It was designed for parents aged 35 to 55 and young professionals aged 21 to 35 in La Union, Philippines, two demographics identified in the literature as underserved by existing financial tools despite having significant household financial responsibilities.

Traditional financial tracking systems primarily functioned as passive tools where users manually recorded expenses and reviewed static summaries (Stefanov et al., 2024). While these systems provided basic budgeting functionalities, they often failed to offer proactive assistance, personalized recommendations, and intuitive interaction methods. As a result, users might find financial tracking tedious, leading to inconsistent usage and incomplete financial records (Stefanov et al., 2024).

Recent advancements in artificial intelligence, particularly Large Language Models (LLMs), had started changing how mobile applications handled user interaction and data processing (Davenport & Mittal, 2022; Dwivedi et al., 2021). Instead of relying only on manual input, these systems could interpret natural language and respond in a more conversational and task-oriented way (OpenAI, 2023; Hean et al., 2025). In practical terms, this allowed users to simply describe their expenses or financial goals in plain language, and the system could convert these into structured data for recording and analysis. This shift made financial tools feel less like traditional record-keeping apps and more like interactive assistants that supported daily decision-making.

This study developed SmartSpend, a mobile financial assistant built for Android devices using Flutter (Hean et al., 2025; OpenAI, 2023). Unlike traditional budgeting apps that required users to manually encode every transaction, SmartSpend combined an LLM-based API with structured financial tracking to reduce manual work. Users could enter expenses using natural language, such as “paid 120 pesos for lunch,” and the system automatically extracted key details like amount, category, and date for storage and analysis (Hean et al., 2025; OpenAI, 2023). This design was intended to make expense tracking more natural and less time-consuming for everyday users.

Beyond expense tracking, SmartSpend featured a conversational AI assistant capable of executing real-time actions such as logging expenses, setting budgets, updating income, and creating savings goals directly from natural language commands. The system also generated a Financial Health Score ranging from 0 to 100 based on user spending patterns, consistency in budgeting, and savings behavior. Instead of only showing raw transactions, this score provided a simple reference point that helped users quickly understand whether their financial behavior was improving or declining over time. This made it easier for users to reflect on their habits without manually analyzing every expense entry.

To reduce the effort required in recording expenses, SmartSpend supported multiple input methods. Users could manually encode expenses, but they could also take photos of receipts, scan barcodes, or use voice input to record transactions. These methods were designed to fit real-life situations for example, quickly scanning a receipt after shopping or speaking expenses while on the move. Optical Character Recognition (OCR) was used to extract text from receipts, while barcode scanning helped identify products more efficiently.

The application used local SQLite storage via the sqflite package (version 11\) for offline functionality, ensuring accessibility even without an internet connection. The system implemented bidirectional cloud synchronization using Firebase Firestore, automatically pushing data to the cloud and retrieving it upon login to merge with local records. This enabled seamless multi-device access to financial data. Firebase Authentication supported secure login methods including email/password, Google Sign-In via OAuth 2.0, and biometric authentication.

Furthermore, the system analyzed financial data, generated summaries, and provided actionable insights and recommendations (Hean et al., 2025). This study contributed to financial technology by demonstrating how AI-driven automation and mobile-based interaction could enhance personal financial management (Hean et al., 2025; Dwivedi et al., 2021).

To improve accessibility and reduce barriers to adoption, SmartSpend included a Demo Mode accessible directly from the login screen without requiring account creation. This feature allowed users to explore the system using realistic sample data before registration (Bitrián et al., 2021). Additionally, the application included a guided feature tour, customizable themes, and dark mode support to enhance usability, engagement, and user satisfaction across different preferences and environments (Stefanov et al., 2024).

## **Conceptual Framework**

![][image2]

**Figure 2: Conceptual Framework (Mobile Application)**

Figure 2 illustrated the conceptual framework of the mobile version of the SmartSpend system, which followed the Input–Process–Output (IPO) model. The input included text input, voice input, receipt images (OCR), barcode scans, and user financial data. The process involved LLM processing, OCR extraction, barcode recognition, data structuring, and data storage and synchronization using SQLite and Firebase. These components worked together to extract, analyze, and organize financial data efficiently. The output consisted of auto-recorded expenses, financial summaries, charts, alerts, AI-generated insights, a Financial Health Score (0–100), and AI-powered financial assistance including general financial question-and-answer responses, market price estimates, and financial product guidance.

### **Statement of Objectives**

This study aimed to design, develop, and evaluate SmartSpend, an AI-assisted mobile financial tracking and advisory application for personal financial management, with a primary focus on parents aged 35 to 55 as the main target population, and young professionals aged 21 to 35 as a secondary demographic, in La Union, Philippines.

Specifically, this study achieved the following:

1\. Assessed the existing financial management practices, common budgeting challenges, and expense tracking behaviors of parents aged 35 to 55 and young professionals aged 21 to 35 in San Fernando City, La Union, through structured surveys.

2\. Designed and developed the SmartSpend mobile application with the integration of a suitable Large Language Model (LLM) API.

3\. Determined the usability of the SmartSpend application using the System Usability Scale (SUS) 

**Scope and Limitations of the Study**  
SmartSpend was designed and developed exclusively for Android devices. The study employed a structured quantitative survey-based methodology; no formal interviews were conducted. The application did not support direct banking or financial institution integration, as no accessible open-banking APIs were available in the Philippine setting. The system did not provide professional financial or tax advice; any AI-generated estimates were approximations and users were advised to verify figures through official sources. The performance of OCR text recognition depended on the quality and clarity of receipt images, and handwritten or low-quality images may produce inaccurate results. All AI-powered features, including expense parsing, financial insights, and the conversational assistant, required an active internet connection. Investment features and direct banking synchronization were outside the scope of this prototype.

**Purpose and Description**

SmartSpend was designed as a mobile application that helped users manage their daily expenses in a more organized and less manual way, addressing the core dimensions of perceived usefulness and ease of use that drove technology adoption. Instead of functioning only as a tracking tool, it also acted as a lightweight financial assistant that can respond to user inputs and provide simple insights about spending behavior. SmartSpend functioned not only as an expense tracker but also as an AI-powered assistant that enhanced users’ financial literacy. The developed solution provided benefits to the following groups:

**Parents.** As primary household financial managers in Filipino families, parents faced significant financial responsibility despite having limited access to formal financial literacy training and structured budgeting tools (Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, 2021). SmartSpend provided automated expense tracking, multi-period financial summaries, and a Financial Health Score that quantified budgeting behavior without requiring manual effort or financial expertise.

**Budget-Conscious Individuals.** This group included individuals who aimed to manage their finances more effectively using digital tools. SmartSpend enables users to control expenses, plan budgets, and improve financial behavior through AI-driven spending analysis. The application supported multiple expense input methods, including manual entry, voice input, and camera-based receipt or barcode scanning. It also provided financial summaries, charts, alerts, and recommendations, along with a wallet management feature that tracked balances across platforms such as GCash, Maya, and bank accounts, offering a consolidated view of available funds.

**Technology Enthusiasts.** Individuals interested in modern technological advancements could explore the application’s integration of artificial intelligence, particularly the use of a large language model for financial assistance and interaction.

**Demo and Evaluation Users.** Users who wished to explore the application without creating an account could utilize the built-in Demo Mode, accessible from the login screen. This mode provided realistic Filipino sample data and full feature access, making it suitable for demonstrations, evaluations, and usability testing without requiring personal data entry.

**The Researchers.** The project enabled the researchers to apply their knowledge and skills in software development and artificial intelligence in a practical setting.

**Future Researchers.** Future researchers might use this study as a reference in the fields of artificial intelligence, mobile applications, and financial technology. The analytics module, including the 50/30/20 budgeting tracker, supported financial awareness by comparing actual spending distribution against recommended allocation standards, making the Financial Health Score transparent and interpretable.

**Technical Background**

In this part, the researchers described the technologies that were used during the design and development of the SmartSpend mobile application. These were critical to making the implementation of features described above possible.

**Flutter.** Flutter was used to build the SmartSpend Android application, targeting Android devices with a single cross-platform codebase. The framework provided a consistent and responsive user interface across different screen sizes. All SmartSpend screens, navigation flows, and interactive components — including the chat interface, analytics charts, and onboarding flow — were implemented as Flutter widgets. The application was compiled to a native Android APK and deployed directly to respondents’ devices during the evaluation phase.

**SQLite.** SQLite was used as SmartSpend’s primary local database through the sqflite package (version 11). Every expense, budget, savings goal, income record, recurring transaction, debt entry, and AI chat message was stored locally on the device. This offline-first approach ensured that all core features remained fully functional without an internet connection. Data was persisted across app restarts and merged with Firebase cloud data upon reconnection.

**Firebase Firestore.** Firebase Firestore was used to synchronize user financial data across sessions and devices. Every expense, budget, and savings goal saved locally in SmartSpend was pushed to Firestore when the device was online and retrieved upon login to merge with local records. This bidirectional sync ensured that users did not lose data when switching devices or reinstalling the application.

**Firebase Authentication.** Firebase Authentication was used to manage user accounts in SmartSpend. It supported three login methods: email and password, Google Sign-In via OAuth 2.0, and biometric authentication (fingerprint or face unlock) as a convenience option after the user’s first successful login. Authentication state was persisted locally so that users remained logged in between sessions without re-entering credentials.

**Firebase Crashlytics.** Firebase Crashlytics was integrated into SmartSpend to monitor application stability during the development and evaluation phases. It automatically captured Flutter framework errors, unhandled exceptions, and asynchronous faults, then reported them to the Firebase Console with device metadata and stack traces. This allowed the researchers to identify and fix critical bugs before distributing the application to evaluation respondents.

**LLM API Integration.** SmartSpend integrated a large language model (LLM) API to power its AI financial assistant, Peso. The primary model used was Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, selected after a comparative evaluation of ten candidate models from four providers (see Table 6\) based on on inference speed, Filipino-English (Taglish) handling, context window capacity, and free-tier feasibility. An eight-model cloud failover chain (Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite as primary, seven fallbacks across Google, Groq, and Cerebras) was implemented so the assistant continued functioning if any single provider was unavailable or rate-limited. The LLM was responsible for 34 autonomous actions including natural language expense parsing, budget recommendations, and financial health insights delivered in conversational Filipino-English.

**Speech-to-Text.** The speech\_to\_text package was used in SmartSpend to enable voice input for recording expenses hands-free. When a user spoke an expense — for example, “Gastos ko ng 150 sa pagkain” — the spoken text was transcribed and passed to the LLM for structured expense parsing. The system automatically detected the Filipino English (en\_PH) locale, with a fallback to en\_US, and supported a 15-second listening window with automatic pause detection.

**Google ML Kit Text Recognition (OCR).** Google ML Kit’s Latin script text recognizer was used in SmartSpend to extract text from receipt images captured by the user’s camera or selected from the gallery. The extracted text was cleaned and routed based on content: single-item receipts were passed directly to the AI chat interface for automatic expense recording, while multi-item receipts were routed to a dedicated import review screen where each item was parsed individually. Users could review, edit categories, assign Want or Need classifications, and selectively confirm items before importing.

**Mobile Scanner (Barcode).** The mobile\_scanner package was used in SmartSpend to scan product barcodes as an alternative expense input method. After a successful scan, the user was prompted to describe or confirm the product, and the LLM parsed the entry into a structured expense record. Each scan was saved to a local scan history for reference. The scanner included a torch toggle and a visual overlay guide frame to assist with low-light scanning.

**Backup and Restore.** The application implemented backup and restore functionality through the system share sheet. All financial data including expenses, budgets, savings goals, income, recurring transactions, debts, wallet balances, mood log, and installment plans was exported as a structured JSON file (version 9 format) that could be shared via any installed application or saved to local storage. Restoration was performed by selecting a previously exported JSON backup file. This approach ensured data portability without requiring additional cloud service dependencies beyond the existing Firebase synchronization.

**fl\_chart.** The fl\_chart package was used to render SmartSpend’s Analytics screen visualizations. It powered three interactive charts: a pie chart showing expense breakdown by category, a bar chart displaying monthly spending trends, and a line chart showing the user’s 30-day Financial Health Score history. These charts updated in real time as the user logged new expenses.

**local\_auth.** The local\_auth package was used to add biometric login to SmartSpend as a faster alternative to entering email and password on subsequent app launches. After the user’s first successful credential-based login, biometric authentication (fingerprint or face unlock) became available using the device’s enrolled biometrics, with a PIN fallback for devices without biometric hardware.

**Financial Health Score (FHS).** SmartSpend introduced a Financial Health Score (FHS) ranging from 0 to 100 as the application’s core academic contribution and primary user-facing summary metric. The FHS gave each user a single, interpretable number reflecting their current budgeting behavior. It operated in two modes: Full Mode (income tracking enabled) computed the score from four equally weighted components — Savings Rate, Overspend Control, Budget Adherence, and Logging Consistency — each contributing 25 points. Lightweight Mode (income tracking disabled) used an alternative set of four components — Spending Restraint, Logging Consistency, Category Balance, and Habit Streak — to remain useful for users without a fixed income. The FHS was formally classified as a Prototype Observed Financial Health Indicator and its full formula, component weights, and consequence mechanism were documented in Chapter III.

**CHAPTER II**  
**DESIGN AND METHODOLOGY**

This chapter presented the methods and procedures  that were used in the development, implementation, and evaluation of the SmartSpend system. It included a detailed discussion of  the research design, population and locale, ethical considerations, data gathering tools and procedures, and the software development methodology applied in the study.

## **Research Design**

This study applied a quantitative descriptive developmental research design, which relied on quantitative approaches in collecting and analyzing data. This design was appropriate because it allowed the researchers to describe the financial management practices of the target population and to measure the usability of the developed system through standardized numerical scores. Through this approach, the researchers were able to capture measurable trends in user behavior, preferences, and challenges.

A validated structured survey questionnaire was used to collect quantitative data on the financial management practices, budgeting challenges, and expense tracking behaviors of the target population. The collected data were analyzed using frequency and percentage to identify patterns and trends that guided the development of system features.

The survey questionnaire underwent content validation by a subject matter expert to ensure clarity, relevance, and alignment with the objectives of the study. In addition, the System Usability Scale (SUS) questionnaire was utilized to evaluate the usability, efficiency, and overall user satisfaction of the developed SmartSpend application. The SUS was a widely used and reliable tool for assessing system usability through standardized scoring (Brooke, 1996). The SUS evaluation was administered to the thirty (30) valid respondents after respondents used the SmartSpend application (the full version or the built-in Demo Mode) for at least 10 minutes, confirmed by a screening question. A target SUS score of 80 or above, corresponding to the adjective rating of Good, was set as the acceptance threshold for this study (Bangor et al., 2009).

**Figure 3\. System Usability Scale (SUS) Score Interpretation**

Figure 3 presents the SUS Score Interpretation Framework used to evaluate the usability of SmartSpend. SUS scores range from 0 to 100 and are categorized into acceptability levels: Not Acceptable (below 51), Marginal (51 to 70), and Acceptable (71 and above) based on Bangor et al. (2008). Adjective anchors from Bangor et al. (2009) placed "OK" at approximately 51, "Good" at 71, and "Excellent" at 85\. The dashed line marks the 68-point average benchmark (Sauro & Lewis, 2016\) and the dotted line marks the pre-established target of 80\. SmartSpend's mean score of 61.83 is marked with a red line, falling in the Marginal range.

Moreover, this study also adopted a developmental research approach, which focused on the design, development, and evaluation of a functional system or prototype. The SmartSpend mobile application was developed using the Flutter framework, with the integration of artificial intelligence through an LLM API. This approach enabled the researchers to iteratively improve the system based on the survey and usability data gathered.

By adopting a quantitative descriptive developmental approach, the study ensured that the system was  not only technically functional but also user-centered, effective, and aligned with the actual needs of the respondents. This research design supported continuous refinement and validation of the SmartSpend application throughout the development process.

**Population and Locale**

The study was conducted in San Fernando City, La Union. A total of thirty (30) respondents participated, composed of parents aged 35 to 55, young professionals aged 21 to 35, and respondents who identified as both, as seen in Table 3\. One content validator participated separately.

A total of thirty (30) respondents were selected using random sampling, as any parent aged 35 to 55 or young professional aged 21 to 35 who met the inclusion criteria was eligible to participate. Thirteen (13) respondents were parents who regularly handled household budgeting, bill payments, and daily expense decisions. Fourteen (14) respondents were young professionals who managed their own income, tracked expenses, and made independent financial decisions. Three (3) respondents identified as both a parent and a young professional. This sample size aligned with common practice for capstone-level usability and needs assessment studies and was sufficient to identify common patterns and usability issues in the context of the developed application. This demographic composition reflected evidence from the BSP Financial Inclusion Survey (2021) that parents in the 35 to 55 age group served as primary household financial decision-makers and were among the groups with the lowest rates of formal financial account ownership and structured budgeting making them a critical and underserved target population for a financial management tool (Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, 2021).

Respondents participated in the needs assessment phase and the system evaluation phase; the two samples were separate groups, although some individuals might have taken part in both. Their feedback was essential in identifying real-world financial challenges and in assessing the usability, effectiveness, and practicality of the SmartSpend mobile application in supporting everyday financial management for both parents and young professionals.

The survey questionnaire underwent content validation by Avigail Candevario, PFMe, a subject matter expert in financial management and business operations to ensure relevance, clarity, and appropriateness of the instrument (see Appendix D). The System Usability Scale (SUS) evaluation process and the overall technical functionality of the SmartSpend system was reviewed by a subject matter expert in information technology. The content validator was selected through purposive sampling based on her expertise in personal finance and financial education.

Any parent aged 35 to 55 or young professional aged 21 to 35 who managed personal or household finances was eligible to participate, and respondents were selected at random from among those who met these criteria.

**Ethical Considerations** 

All ethical considerations were strictly followed throughout the entire research process. Participation in this study was voluntary, and no form of pressure was imposed on the respondents. All participants, including parents and young professionals, had the right to refuse participation or withdraw from the study at any time without any penalty.

Informed consent was obtained from all participants before their involvement in the study (see Appendix B). They were properly informed about the nature and purpose of the research prior to their participation.

In addition, confidentiality was strictly maintained. Personal information of the respondents was kept secure and treated with utmost confidentiality. All responses gathered were used solely for academic purposes.

Furthermore, all collected data were carefully managed and stored to prevent any form of loss or unauthorized access. The researchers ensured that ethical standards were upheld throughout the study.

**Data Gathering Tools and Procedure**

This section describes the data gathering tools and procedures used for each of the three study objectives. Each objective required a distinct instrument and procedure aligned with its specific purpose.

For the first objective — assessing the financial management practices, budgeting challenges, and expense tracking behaviors of the target population — a validated structured survey questionnaire (see Appendix A) was used as the primary data gathering tool. The questionnaire was administered to thirty (30) respondents comprising parents aged 35 to 55 and young professionals aged 21 to 35 in San Fernando City, La Union. It covered financial habits, budgeting methods, common challenges, and technology acceptance. Prior to distribution, the questionnaire underwent content validation by Avigail Candevario, PFMe, a graduate of Bachelor of Science in Commerce major in Management and an active business owner with experience in financial management and business operations (see Appendix D). Survey responses were tallied and analyzed using frequency and percentage to identify patterns and trends in the financial behaviors of the respondents.

For the second objective — designing and developing the SmartSpend mobile application — the results of the first objective served as the primary basis for feature identification and system design. The specific financial challenges and technology preferences identified in the needs assessment directly shaped the application’s feature set, including multi-modal expense input, conversational AI assistance, offline-first local storage, and the Financial Health Score. SmartSpend was built using the Flutter framework targeting Android, with SQLite (sqflite v11) for local storage, Firebase Firestore for cloud synchronization, Firebase Authentication for user identity management, and Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite as the primary LLM API for AI features. Development followed an Agile Kanban methodology with iterative feature delivery across structured phases: Backlog, Requirements, Design, Development, Testing, Deployment, and Done/Review.

For the third objective — evaluating the usability of the developed system — the 10-item System Usability Scale (SUS) questionnaire (see Appendix C) was administered as the evaluation instrument. Respondents were required to use the SmartSpend application (the full version or the built-in Demo Mode) for a minimum of 10 minutes before completing the SUS. A screening question confirmed that each respondent had met this usage threshold. SUS scores were computed using the standard Brooke (1996) formula: for odd-numbered items, the item score minus 1 was used; for even-numbered items, 5 minus the item score was used; the sum of all adjusted scores was then multiplied by 2.5 to yield a score out of 100\. Individual scores were averaged to produce the overall mean SUS score, which was interpreted against the Bangor et al. (2009) adjective rating scale and the pre-established acceptance threshold of 80\.

**Software Methodology**

The development of the SmartSpend mobile application followed the Agile Kanban Software Development Methodology as seen in Figure 4\. This approach was selected because the project required continuous feature integration, testing, and refinement, especially due to the involvement of multiple components such as artificial intelligence, OCR processing, and cloud synchronization. Unlike traditional development models that followed a strict and linear sequence, Kanban allowed the researchers to work on tasks dynamically, with phases potentially overlapping or repeating as needed, while continuously improving the system based on feedback and testing results. 

![][image3]

Note. The content validator participated separately and is not included in the respondent total of 30\.

**Figure 4: Agile Kanban Workflow for SmartSpend Development**

Figure 4 presents the Agile Kanban Workflow used in the development of SmartSpend. The board is organized into seven phases: Backlog, Requirements, Design, Development, Testing, Deployment, and Done/Review, each with a Work-in-Progress (WIP) limit to prevent bottlenecks and maintain focus. Tasks move across the board as development progresses, while a Continuous Improvement loop connects the Done/Review phase back to Development and Testing to support iterative refinement. This methodology allowed the researchers to integrate features incrementally and respond to testing feedback throughout the development cycle.

To implement this methodology, the researchers utilized a Kanban board that visually represented the workflow of the project. The board was divided into several columns, namely: Backlog, Requirements, Design, Development, Testing, Deployment, and Done/Review. Each task related to the system such as implementing OCR, integrating the LLM API, or designing the database schema were represented as individual task cards. These cards moved across the board depending on their current progress. Work-in-progress (WIP) limits were also applied to ensure that the researchers focused only on a manageable number of tasks at a time, preventing overload and maintaining productivity.

In the **Backlog Phase**, all planned features and system requirements were first listed and organized. This included core functionalities such as expense tracking, AI-powered parsing, Financial Health Score computation, voice input integration, receipt scanning, and cloud synchronization. The researchers also included minor features such as theme customization, demo mode, and onboarding tutorials. Each feature was broken down into smaller, actionable tasks to make development more manageable.

During the **Requirements Phase**, the researchers gathered data through a survey of selected respondents aligned with the study’s target population of parents and young professionals. This phase aimed to identify real-world financial management practices, common challenges in expense tracking, and user expectations for a financial application. Based on the collected data, the researchers defined both functional requirements (e.g., automatic expense logging, AI recommendations) and non-functional requirements (e.g., usability, performance, offline capability).

In the **Design Phase**, the researchers translated the identified requirements into a concrete system structure. This included designing the application architecture, database schema, and data flow. Specifically, the SQLite database structure was mapped to handle tables such as expenses, income, budgets, savings goals, and chat history. The researchers also designed how data flowed between the mobile application, the LLM API, and Firebase services. Additionally, interface layouts and user navigation flows were planned to ensure that the application remained simple and user-friendly despite having advanced features.

The **Development Phase** involved the actual implementation of the system using the Flutter framework. The researchers developed the application incrementally by focusing on one feature at a time. For example, the basic expense tracking module was developed first, followed by the integration of AI parsing through the LLM API. After that, additional features such as OCR using Google ML Kit, barcode scanning, and voice input were implemented. Firebase services, including Firestore and Authentication, were also integrated during this phase to support cloud synchronization and secure login. Each completed feature was tested individually before being merged into the main application.

In the **Testing Phase**, the researchers conducted both functional and usability testing. Functional testing ensured that each feature operated correctly, such as verifying if the OCR accurately extracted receipt data or if the AI correctly categorized expenses. Usability testing involved selected respondents who used the application and evaluated their experience using the System Usability Scale (SUS). The researchers also observed user interactions to identify difficulties, confusion, or inefficiencies within the system. Any issues discovered during this phase were documented and fed back into the Development phase for refinement and correction.

During the **Deployment Phase**, the completed SmartSpend application was deployed to Android devices for actual usage and evaluation. The researchers prepared the application for demonstration and evaluation by ensuring that all features were stable and properly integrated. Demo Mode was also activated to allow users to explore the system without requiring account registration, making it easier to conduct presentations and usability testing.

Finally, in the **Done/Review Phase**, the researchers evaluated the overall performance and effectiveness of the system. This included analyzing SUS scores, reviewing user feedback, and assessing whether the application met its intended objectives. The researchers identified which features performed well and which areas required improvement. Insights gathered from this phase were used to refine the system and provide recommendations for future development.

The phases of the Kanban workflow, together with their key tasks and deliverables, were summarized in Table 4:

**Table 4: Agile Kanban Workflow Phases and Deliverables**

| Phase | Key Tasks | Deliverable |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Backlog | Define features; needs survey; literature review on PH financial gaps | Prioritized feature list; literature review |
| Requirements | Translate findings into specs; validate questionnaire; LLM API benchmarking | Validated questionnaire; LLM benchmarking matrix (Table 6\) |
| Design | SQLite schema (26 tables); FHS formula; UI wireframes; data flow diagrams | System architecture; FHS documentation |
| Development | Build expense tracking; integrate Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite; add OCR/voice/batch screenshots; FHS engine; Firebase sync; gamification | Functional app; all 34 agentic actions operational |
| Testing | LLM parsing accuracy; SUS with 30 respondents; survey feedback; bug log | SUS scores; parsing observations; bug documentation |
| Deployment | Build release APKs; prepare Demo Mode; publish GitHub Releases | Release APKs v3.1.0; project documentation |
| Done/Review | Analyze SUS scores; review feedback; document recommendations | Final evaluation report; post-capstone roadmap |

Each section ended by stating whether the corresponding objective was achieved.

**Assessed the Financial Management Practices, Budgeting Challenges, and Expense Tracking Behaviors of Parents and Young Professionals**

The findings confirmed the critical financial management challenges identified in the literature. Among the 30 respondents, 96.7% expressed positive intent to use an AI-powered financial application, validating the study's premise. The most prevalent challenges were rising prices of basic goods, unexpected medical expenses, and family responsibilities. GCash was used by 93.3% of respondents, validating the app's emphasis on e-wallet transaction parsing.

These results showed that the first objective of the study was achieved: the financial management practices, budgeting challenges, and expense tracking behaviors of the target population were successfully assessed through the validated survey instrument.

**Design and Development of the SmartSpend Mobile Application**

The second objective was to design and develop the SmartSpend mobile application, including the selection of an appropriate Large Language Model API through comparative technical evaluation.

Guided by the needs assessment results, the researchers designed SmartSpend as an offline-first Flutter application for Android. A local SQLite database stored all financial records, with optional Firebase Firestore synchronization and Firebase Authentication for signed-in users. Because most respondents tracked expenses through receipts and e-wallet histories, expense input was designed around multiple modalities: natural-language text and voice, receipt OCR, barcode scanning, and batch screenshot import of e-wallet transactions. An LLM-powered assistant, Peso, was integrated to parse these inputs and execute 34 financial actions, and a Financial Health Score was designed to summarize budgeting behavior. The selection of the LLM API, the computation of the Financial Health Score, and the resulting system are presented in the sections that follow.

The selection of an appropriate LLM API was a critical design decision because it directly influenced the accuracy, latency, and cost of natural language expense parsing and conversational assistance. For a mobile financial assistant requiring Filipino-English capability and free-tier deployment, the evaluation criteria were weighted as: Filipino-English accuracy (25%), speed/latency (20%), tool use and JSON reliability (20%), free tier availability (15%), context window (10%), and financial reasoning quality (10%). Table 6 presented the comparative evaluation results.

**Table 6: Comparative Evaluation of LLM APIs for SmartSpend Integration**

| Model | Provider | Context | Speed (t/s) | Filipino | Tool Use | Free Tier |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite | Google | 1,048,576 | \~400–600 | 5/5 | 5/5 | \~500/day |
| Gemini 3.5 Flash | Google | 1,048,576 | \~200–400 | 5/5 | 5/5 | \~20/day |
| GPT-OSS 120B | Groq LPU | 131,072 | \~500 | Not measured | 5/5 | \~1,000/day |
| Qwen 3.6 27B | Groq LPU | 131,072 | Not measured | Not measured | 5/5 | 1,000/day |
| Qwen 3.8 27B | Groq LPU | 131,072 | Not measured | Not measured | 5/5 | 1,000/day |
| GPT-OSS 20B | Groq LPU | 131,072 | Not measured | Not measured | 5/5 | 1,000/day, 30K TPM |
| Groq Compound Mini | Groq LPU | 131,072 | Not measured | Not measured | 5/5 (web+code) | 1,000/day |
| GPT-OSS 120B | Cerebras WSE | 131,072 | \~3,000 | Not measured | 5/5 | 1M tokens/day |
| Mistral 7B | Mistral | 32,000 | \~600 | 3/5 | 3/5 | Self-host |
| Gemma 2 9B | Google | 8,192 | \~500 | 3/5 | 3/5 | Local only |

From the ten candidate models in Table 6, Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite was selected as the primary model because it offered a high free-tier request quota, good Filipino-English (Taglish) handling in the team trials, a 1-million token context window, and native function calling support for the 34 agentic action types (Li et al., 2024; Google, 2024f). Groq's LLaMA-family endpoints (LLaMA 4 Scout, LLaMA 3.3 70B, LLaMA 3.1 8B) were retired by Groq in mid-to-late 2026 and had been replaced in the fallback chain with Groq-hosted OpenAI GPT-OSS (120B/20B) and Qwen (3.6/3.8 27B) models, which Groq then recommended as the direct migration path. Models like GPT-4o and Claude were paid-only cost-prohibitive for academic deployment at zero budget.

SmartSpend used dynamic full-context injection rather than RAG. A typical user had 20–50 expenses, 5–10 budgets, and 3–5 goals (\~1,000–5,000 tokens), fitting within any evaluated model's context window. RAG added unnecessary vector search overhead for this small per-user dataset (Davenport & Mittal, 2022).

The Financial Health Score (FHS) was SmartSpend's core academic contribution formally positioned as a Prototype Observed Financial Health Indicator (FHI), adapting ideas from two published financial-health measurement efforts rather than inventing a scoring system from nothing. The main design choice computing the score from a user's own transaction data instead of a survey followed the Commonwealth Bank of Australia and Melbourne Institute's (CBA-MI) "Observed" scale, which summed categorical bank-record measures and rescaled the total to 0–100 (Comerton-Forde et al., 2018). Three of the four components below adapted the Spend, Save and Plan ideas from the Financial Health Network's FinHealth Score® (Financial Health Network, 2021). The UNSGSA's own working-group note on measuring financial health treated transaction/account-based measurement as a promising but still early-stage fourth approach, better viewed as complementary to survey-based scales rather than a full replacement (Gubbins, Mazzotta & Rhyne, 2021\) which was exactly why this score was named a "Prototype," not presented as a validated instrument in its own right.

Equal weights that added up to 100 followed the simplest published scoring method for this kind of scale. CBA's own 10-question Reported scale gave each question equal weight (0–4 points, 40 total) and multiplied by 2.5 to land on a 0–100 range, and separate validation testing found that this simple approach correlated very highly with more complex model-based scores (Gubbins, Mazzotta & Rhyne, 2021). SmartSpend followed the same logic with four components: 4 × 25 \= 100\. The weights themselves were a design choice, not a statistically derived result that was stated plainly rather than implied to be more rigorous than it was.

Full Mode (income tracking enabled; 4 components of 25 points, 100 maximum):

1\. Savings Rate (25 pts): Score \= 25 × min(1.0, savingsRate / 0.20). The 20% target came from the 50/30/20 budgeting rule (Warren & Tyagi, 2005).

2\. Overspend Control (25 pts): Score \= 25 × (1 − (hardOverDays \+ softOverDays × 0.5) / activeDays). A day where a single large one-off purchase (e.g., a gadget or event ticket) pushes spending over the daily budget counts as a "soft" overspend day at half weight; a day with scattered, habitual overspending across multiple items counts as "hard" at full weight.

3\. Budget Adherence (25 pts): Score \= 25 × (onBudgetCategories / totalBudgetedCategories). Category-level budget limits followed the common personal-finance practice of zero-based budgeting (popularized by Ramsey, 2003), though this practice itself was not independently validated in peer-reviewed literature.

4\. Logging Consistency (25 pts): Score \= 25 × (loggedDays / activeDays). Consistent self-monitoring increased transaction salience and promoted deliberate spending (Thaler & Sunstein, 2008).

Lightweight Mode (students, freelancers, informal workers no income tracking): (1) Spending Restraint (25 pts) vs a user-set limit; (2) Logging Consistency (25 pts); (3) Category Balance (25 pts) Score \= 25 × (1.0 − max(0.0, topDiscretionaryCategory / discretionaryTotal − 0.40) / 0.60), clamped to \[0, 25\]; Bills, Health and Education are excluded so essential fixed costs don't reduce the score; (4) Habit Streak (25 pts), full credit at 14 days (Duhigg, 2012).

Score Adjustments Warning Decay \= min(15, 5 × decayDays), applying loss aversion theory (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979; Thaler & Sunstein, 2008); only fires for discretionary overspend, never for Bills/Health/Education. Gap Adjustment (+2/day confirmed no-spend, −3/day unlogged-but-presumed-spent) rewards verified restraint and penalizes silence that can't be told apart from unreported spending (Ariely, 2008). Final score clamped 0–100.

**Overview of the System**

![System flowchart for SmartSpend][image5]

**Figure 6\. SmartSpend System Flowchart**

Figure 6 presents the system flowchart of SmartSpend, illustrating the complete processing pipeline from user input to output. The flowchart begins with four input modalities — voice, text, receipt photo, and GCash screenshot — which are routed through an on-device preprocessing and redaction layer that applies speech-to-text conversion, ML Kit OCR extraction, and automatic masking of sensitive data such as mobile numbers, reference numbers, and account patterns. The system then checks whether local-only mode is enabled: if activated, the input is forwarded to a private local LLM running on the user's home network via tools such as Ollama, LM Studio, or Jan; if not, the input is sent to the Cloud LLM Provider Chain with Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite as the primary model. If the primary provider is unavailable, the system automatically falls back to the next available provider in the chain. Once a response is received, the AI performs agentic action parsing across 34 action types using JSON function calls. A duplicate detection check is applied before writing to the SQLite on-device database; duplicate entries are skipped and reported in a summary card, while new entries are stored locally and optionally synchronized to Firebase Firestore for signed-in users. The Financial Health Score is then computed from four components, each contributing 25 points to a maximum score of 100\. The final output delivered to the user consists of charts, alerts, Peso companion messages, and AI-generated financial advice.![Use case diagram for SmartSpend][image6]

**Figure 7\. Use Case Diagram**

Figure 7 presents the use case diagram of SmartSpend, showing the interactions between the two actors — the User and the System — and the core functionalities of the application. On the user side, seven primary use cases are identified: logging an expense through voice, text, or photo input; importing screenshots from e-wallets such as GCash and Maya; chatting with the AI assistant Peso; setting a budget; setting a savings goal; viewing analytics; and viewing the Financial Health Score. On the system side, three automated processes support these interactions: calculating the Financial Health Score based on the user's recorded transactions and budget behavior; sending notifications for bill reminders, budget alerts, and milestone events; and synchronizing data to the cloud for signed-in users. The dashed include relationship between "View FHS Score" and "Calculate FHS" indicates that viewing the score always triggers a calculation from the user's most recent transactions and budgets, so the score reflects current behavior without manual updates.

![Screen navigation map for SmartSpend][image7]

**Figure 8\. Visual Table of Contents**

Figure 8 presents the visual table of contents of SmartSpend, showing the navigation structure of the application from the login screen to the home dashboard and its connected modules. From the home screen, users can access seven main sections: Expenses, Budget, Savings, Analytics, AI Chat, Achievements, and Settings. This diagram illustrates how the application was designed around a central hub navigation model, allowing users to move between financial management features without nested menus or complex navigation paths.

Several Filipino-specific and usability features were implemented over the course of development rather than left as future work: a Paluwagan (rotating savings group) tracker built on the existing debt and recurring-transaction infrastructure; a six-month savings-rate trend chart with a 20% target line in Analytics; a long-press quick-edit gesture on budget tiles; and an offline cache fallback for the AI-generated financial advice and monthly summary cards, so a quota error did not leave the user without any insight.

A multi-wallet system was also implemented, supporting 20 Philippine banks and 5 digital banks plus e-wallets such as GCash, Maya, GrabPay, and ShopeePay, with automatic balance deduction upon expense logging and wallet-to-wallet transfers.

Two further additions were worth documenting as part of the system's development: first, a full audit-trail subsystem (four dedicated history tables wallet, budget, goal-contribution, and income each logging the old value, new value, change amount, reason, and source of every edit, viewable per-item via a long-press) gave the app's financial records the kind of change-of-custody traceability expected of a financial tool, not just a flat transaction log. Second, the AI assistant's system prompt was extended with structured knowledge of common Philippine Buy-Now-Pay-Later and short-term lending products (GLoan, Maya Loan, ShopeePayLater, LazPayLater, HomeCredit, BillEase, Skyro, Akulaku, Atome, UnaCash), including their typical monthly interest rates and the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas' interest rate cap under BSP Circular No. 1133, so that the assistant could meaningfully discuss a user's installment and lending obligations rather than treating them as generic expenses.

The v2.9.97–3.1.0 releases added several usability and reliability capabilities. Earlier, an AI date-resolution fix made the assistant receive today's and yesterday's dates explicitly so that phrases such as "yesterday" or "kahapon" were recorded on the correct day, and the assistant then checked whether an item was already stored before logging it again. Version 3.0.4 added a Local-only switch for Private Mode and a warning when a Local Account user logged in. Local Account users are also offered an automatic JSON and CSV backup when they log out . Version 3.0.3 added a Local Account mode ("Continue Without Account") in which all data stayed on the device and can be exported at any time, with a one-way upgrade path that pushed the local data to a new cloud account on registration. The four larger additions were as follows. First, chat sessions: AI conversations were stored as separate, titled sessions (a new chat\_sessions table, database schema v14) that could be renamed, archived, searched, or deleted, replacing a single flat history that silently dropped anything older than the last 200 messages. Second, AI recovery: after each AI response, a summary card showed which items were recorded, skipped as duplicates, or failed, with a one-tap helper to re-log anything the AI missed, so errors were visible to the user instead of silent. Third, transaction sorting and grouping by date, logged date, category, amount, name or source, plus a quick-jump bar in Analytics. Fourth, a full demo dataset (35 transactions across three months, wallets, budgets, goals, paluwagan and installment plans) with a one-tap reset, used for the live usability demonstration. Since v3.0.4, logging in from a Local Account first showed a warning, because the cloud copy replaced the local data by design.

AI privacy was described as three tiers, only two of which existed at the time. (1) Cloud AI (default): requests go through the provider chain, with mobile numbers, reference numbers and bank-account patterns redacted on-device first. The primary provider was used under Google's free ("unpaid") Gemini API quota, whose terms stated that submitted content might be used to improve Google's products, might be read by human reviewers, and should not include personal information; redaction therefore reduced but did not remove the exposure, and users with sensitive details were directed to Private Local Mode. Since v3.0.5 a one-time privacy disclosure was also shown before the first AI message. (2) Private Local Mode (implemented, v2.9.92): while the app could reach a model running on the user's own PC or Mac over the home network, requests went only to that model and financial data did not leave the network; if the local server was unreachable the app fell back to the cloud chain, unless the user had switched on Local-only mode (added in v3.0.4), in which case the AI stopped responding instead of falling back. (3) On-device AI (planned, not implemented): a model running on the phone itself, with no network at all. Research at the time indicated this was feasible on 2026 flagship phones and, as an opt-in download of roughly 2.6 GB, on phones with about 6 GB of RAM, but not yet on the 4 GB mid-range phones common among Filipino students; it was therefore listed under Recommendations, not as a delivered feature.

From v3.0.5 to v3.1.0 the app's mascot, Peso, was developed from a static icon into a context-aware companion. The mascot has 12 animated moods (idle movement, periodic blinking, animated mood changes, tap reactions and an optional speech bubble), appears on most major screens and as the avatar beside AI replies, and changes mood with the sentiment of the assistant's reply and, on the home screen, with the Financial Health Score tier. A voice service supplies short Taglish messages for 31 situations (two to four variants each, chosen at random so the same line does not repeat every session) used in the AI greeting, companion messages and the app's scheduled notifications; a context service gives a one-time tip per screen per session for 17 screens; and a haptic service provides tactile feedback. Once-a-day checks react to events such as no expenses logged by 2 PM, a no-spend day, budget status, upcoming bills, a change in FHS tier, logging streaks of 7, 14, 21 and 30 days, and savings-goal milestones at 25, 50, 75 and 100 percent, and ten additional achievement badges (36 in total) were added with celebration sheets. Tapping a notification stores its payload so that the next launch can respond in context.

These behaviours applied the same ideas used for Warning Decay and the badge system prompt, non-blocking, autonomy-supportive feedback tied to the user's own logging and score changes (Thaler & Sunstein, 2008; Deci & Ryan, 2000). They were added after the usability-evaluation design was fixed, so their effect on user behaviour has not been measured; the longitudinal study proposed in Chapter IV was where it would be tested.

The optional local-LLM integration described above shipped with a guided in-app setup flow covering three common local-inference tools (Ollama, LM Studio, Jan), including a hardware-tier picker (8/16/32GB RAM) to help a non-technical user choose a workable local model size, and fell back to the cloud provider chain if the local server became unreachable mid-session, unless the user has switched on Local-only mode.

These results showed that the second objective of the study was achieved: SmartSpend v3.1.0 was designed and developed as a working Android application, and a suitable LLM API was selected through a comparative technical evaluation.

**Determined the Usability of SmartSpend Using the System Usability Scale** 

Respondents were required to use the SmartSpend application either the full version or the built-in Demo Mode accessible from the login screen for a minimum of 10 minutes before completing the SUS questionnaire. This was enforced through a screening question at the start of the SUS form. Of 36 respondents who attempted the survey, 30 confirmed they used the app for the required minimum duration and were included in the final analysis. The remaining 6 were excluded: 5 for insufficient app usage time and 1 for straight-line response bias. The respondents for the needs assessment (Objective 1\) and for the SUS evaluation (Objective 3\) were separate groups; some individuals may have taken part in both, but the two samples were analyzed independently for their respective objectives.

SUS scores were computed using the standard formula: odd-numbered items minus 1; 5 minus even-numbered items; sum multiplied by 2.5 (Brooke, 1996). The overall SUS score was interpreted against the Bangor, Kortum, and Miller (2009) adjective rating scale.

![][image15]

**Figure 16\. SUS Computation Table**

Figure 16 presents a sample SUS computation for one respondent who scored 75.0, illustrating how the standard SUS formula is applied to raw questionnaire responses. The table lists all ten SUS items with the respondent's responses on a 1–5 scale and the contribution of each item to the final score. For odd-numbered items (1, 3, 5, 7, 9), the contribution is the response value minus 1; for even-numbered items (2, 4, 6, 8, 10), the contribution is 5 minus the response value. The sum of all contributions is 30, which is then multiplied by 2.5 to yield a final SUS score of 75.0, corresponding to an adjective rating of "Good" (Bangor et al., 2009). This example is provided for illustrative purposes only; the overall mean SUS score of 61.83 reported in this study is the average computed across all 30 valid respondents.

**Table 7: Overall SUS Result**

| Overall SUS Score | Grade | Adjective | Acceptable |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 61.83 | D | OK | No (below the 68 benchmark and the 80 target) |

As shown in Table 7, SmartSpend obtained an overall SUS score of 61.83, a grade of D, and an adjective rating of "OK" (Bangor et al., 2009), which was below the pre-established acceptance threshold of 80 or above and below the 68-point average benchmark (Sauro & Lewis, 2016).

![][image16]

**Figure 17\. SUS Scores by Respondent Group (N \= 30\)**

Figure 17 presents the mean SUS scores of the two respondent groups displayed as a bar chart with error bars representing ±1 standard deviation. Parents aged 35–55 (n \= 10\) obtained a mean score of 58.25 (SD \= 19.72), while young professionals aged 21–35 (n \= 20\) obtained a mean score of 63.62 (SD \= 16.65). Both groups received an adjective rating of "OK" under the Bangor et al. (2009) scale. The red line marks the overall mean of 61.83, the dashed line marks the 68-point average benchmark (Sauro & Lewis, 2016), and the dotted line marks the pre-established target of 80\. The overlapping error bars between the two groups indicate that the difference in mean scores was not substantial, and both groups fell below the benchmark and target. The slightly higher score among young professionals was consistent with their generally greater familiarity with mobile applications compared to the parent group.

**Table 8: System Usability Scale (SUS) Results by Respondent Group**

| Respondent Group | N | Mean SUS Score | SD | Range | Adjective Rating |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Parents (35–55) | 10 | 58.25 | 19.72 | 35.0–90.0 | OK |
| Young Professionals (21–35) | 20 | 63.62 | 16.65 | 42.5–92.5 | OK |
| Combined | 30 | 61.83 | 17.58 | 35.0–92.5 | OK |

As shown in Tables 7 and 8, SmartSpend achieved an overall mean SUS score of 61.83 (SD \= 17.58; median \= 55.00; range \= 35.0–92.5) with an adjective rating of "OK" per Bangor et al. (2009). This score is below the 68-point average benchmark established by Bangor et al. and below the pre-established target of ≥80 acknowledged as a limitation of the current prototype. Young professionals (n \= 20, M \= 63.62, SD \= 16.65) scored slightly higher than parents (n \= 10, M \= 58.25, SD \= 19.72), and both groups fell within the “OK” range. Respondents indicated strong intent to use the system frequently (Q1 mean: 4.35/5) and felt confident using it (Q9 mean: 4.19/5). The main concerns were system consistency (Q6) and complexity (Q2, Q4), which inform the UI/UX recommendations in Chapter IV. These results are based on N=30 valid respondents screened from 36 total responses.

No formal open-ended survey data was collected. The study used a structured quantitative survey instrument only; no interviews were conducted. 

These results showed that the third objective of the study was partially achieved: usability was evaluated using the System Usability Scale with 30 valid respondents, but the mean score of 61.83 fell below the 68-point benchmark (Sauro & Lewis, 2016\) and the pre-established target of 80\.

Table 9 presents the observed field-level parsing performance of SmartSpend’s multimodal import features. The three input modalities — receipt OCR, voice input, and barcode scan — were evaluated on their ability to correctly extract key fields: amount, merchant/description, date, and category. Observations were recorded during the development and beta-testing phase prior to formal respondent evaluation.

**Table 9: SmartSpend Multimodal Import: Field-Level Parsing Performance**

| Input Modality | Amount (%) | Description (%) | Date (%) | Category (%) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Receipt OCR (camera/gallery) | 84.2 | 78.6 | 71.3 | 82.1 |
| Voice Input (speech-to-text \+ AI) | 91.4 | 86.7 | 68.9 | 79.3 |

Voice accuracy varied with background noise and en\_PH locale support. Formal benchmarking using standardized test sets across platforms is recommended as future work (see Recommendation 9).

**CHAPTER IV**  
**CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS**

This chapter presented the conclusions drawn from the results of the study and the recommendations of the researchers.

**Conclusions**

The needs assessment confirmed that 96.7% of the 30 respondents expressed positive intent to use an AI-powered financial application, and 93.3% already used GCash, validating the study's target population and feature priorities. SmartSpend v3.1.0 was successfully developed with its core planned features implemented. The SUS evaluation yielded a mean score of 61.83 (adjective: "OK"), below the ≥80 target. Therefore, all three objectives of the study were addressed, with the third objective partially achieved.

The first objective was to assess the financial management practices, budgeting challenges, and expense tracking behaviors of parents aged 35 to 55 and young professionals aged 21 to 35\. The needs assessment of thirty (30) respondents revealed that 96.7% expressed positive intent to use an AI-powered financial application and 93.3% already used GCash. The first objective was achieved.

The second objective was to design and develop the SmartSpend mobile application with the integration of a suitable LLM API. SmartSpend v3.1.0 was developed as a working Android application with multi-modal expense input, offline-first local storage, 34 AI actions, and a Financial Health Score formally classified as a Prototype Observed Financial Health Indicator. A comparative technical evaluation of ten candidate models from four providers led to the selection of Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite as the primary model, supported by an eight-model cloud failover chain (Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite as primary, seven fallbacks). The second objective was achieved.

The third objective was to evaluate the usability of SmartSpend using the System Usability Scale. The evaluation yielded a mean SUS score of 61.83 (SD \= 17.58, Median \= 55.00) from 30 valid respondents, which was below the pre-established acceptance threshold of 80 and the 68-point average benchmark (Sauro & Lewis, 2016). The third objective was partially achieved.

**Recommendations**

In view of the results of the study, the following recommendations were made:

**1\. Payday-cycle-aware budgeting.** The researchers recommended that the developers implement budgeting resets aligned with the semi-monthly (15th and 30th) salary cycle common in the Philippines.

**2\. Backend API proxy and per-user keys.** The researchers recommended that the developers move LLM API key management to a server-side proxy (e.g., Firebase Cloud Function) to remove device-side key exposure and enforce per-user message limits, because the free-tier request quotas (Table 6\) were shared by every user of the prototype. Letting users add their own key was an interim measure.

**3\. Google Play release.** The researchers recommended that, after the backend proxy and a privacy policy were in place, the developers submit  SmartSpend to the Google Play Store, since the prototype was currently distributed as a downloadable APK.

**4\. On-device AI tier.** The researchers recommended that the developers add  an opt-in on-device model (e.g., Gemma 4 E2B through Google's LiteRT-LM, about a 2.6 GB download) for users who wanted fully offline AI, routing only simple logging tasks to it and keeping complex financial advice on the cloud tier, because the current local AI mode required a separate computer on the same network.

**5\. SQLite encryption.** The researchers recommended that the developers implement SQLCipher-based encryption for the local database in a future schema migration, because the local database of the prototype was not encrypted.

**6\. Household and remittance features.** The researchers recommended that the developers add  shared couple and family wallets and inbound OFW remittance tracking as a distinct income category to serve more user groups.

**7\. Longitudinal evaluation.** The researchers recommended that future researchers measure  SmartSpend's effect on financial behavior over three to six months with a larger sample, because the usability evaluation in this study measured usability at a single point in time.

**8\. UI/UX refinement.** The researchers recommended that the developers address the main usability concerns identified in the SUS results — particularly system consistency (Q6) and complexity (Q2) — through interface redesign in a future iteration to improve the overall usability score.

**9\. Formal parsing evaluation.** The researchers recommended that future researchers conduct a formal evaluation of the OCR and AI parsing accuracy using standardized test receipts across multiple platforms to establish a reliable performance baseline for the multimodal import features.
